arXiv:2605.25428v2 [math.NT] 24 Sep 2026

Lubin-Tate representations over nontrivial finite Galois extensions of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} are not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate

Kaiji Kondo Address: Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences, Kyoto University, Kyoto 606-8502, JAPAN Email address: kkondo@kurims.kyoto-u.ac.jp
Abstract.

In the present paper, we show that, for a prime number pp and a nontrivial finite Galois extension kk of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, under the additional assumption that −1∈k\sqrt{-1}\in k if p=2p=2, the continuous pp-adic representation of the absolute Galois group GkG_{k} determined by a Lubin-Tate formal group over the ring of integers of kk has the following property: for almost all outer automorphisms of GkG_{k}, its composite with a representative of the outer automorphism is not Hodge-Tate. More precisely, the set of outer automorphisms for which the resulting representation is Hodge-Tate is contained in a closed subgroup of Out⁡(Gk)\operatorname{Out}(G_{k}) of Haar measure zero. In particular, this representation is not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate [in the sense of Hoshi]. In the case where pp is odd, this settles the odd-degree cases left open in the previous works of Hoshi and the author and, together with the known even-degree case, completes the picture for finite Galois extensions of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}. This exhibits a sharp contrast, from the viewpoint of anabelian geometry, between the pp-adic cyclotomic character and other pp-adic Lubin-Tate characters.

Key words and phrases: 
anabelian geometry, Aut-intrinsic Hodge-Tate-ness, Lubin-Tate characters, abelian Hodge-Tate representations, mapping class groups

Introduction

Let pp be a prime number, kk a finite extension of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, and k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk. We write Gk=defGal⁡(k¯/k)G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\Gal(\overline{k}/k) for the absolute Galois group of kk determined by the algebraic closure k¯\overline{k}. In anabelian geometry, it is natural to discuss conditions for a continuous automorphism of GkG_{k} to be induced by a field automorphism of kk [cf., e.g., [4], [11]]. The following theorem studies such conditions from the perspective of pp-adic Hodge theory:

Theorem A ([4], Corollary 3.4).

Let α:Gk⟶∼Gk\alpha\colon G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}G_{k} be a continuous automorphism of GkG_{k}. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    The automorphism α\alpha is induced by a field automorphism of kk.

  2. (2)

    For every finite-dimensional continuous pp-adic representation ρ:Gk→GLn⁡(ℚp)\rho\colon G_{k}\to\GL_{n}(\mathbb{Q}_{p}) of GkG_{k} that is Hodge-Tate, the composite Gk→αGk→ρGLn⁡(ℚp)G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\alpha}}{{\to}}G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho}}{{\to}}\GL_{n}(\mathbb{Q}_{p}) is Hodge-Tate.

  3. (3)

    The automorphism α\alpha is of HT-qLT-type [cf. [4], Definition 1.3, (ii)\rm(\hskip 0.80002ptii\hskip 0.80002pt)].

As suggested by this theorem and [4], Definition 1.3, (ii)\rm(\hskip 0.80002ptii\hskip 0.80002pt), Lubin-Tate characters play an important role in the study of the geometricity [i.e., the condition to be induced by a field automorphism] of continuous automorphisms of GkG_{k}.

Moreover, motivated by this theorem, Hoshi defined the following notion for continuous pp-adic representations.

Definition ([7], Definition 1.3).

Let VV be a finite-dimensional ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-vector space and ρ:Gk→Autℚp⁡(V)\rho\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(V) a continuous pp-adic representation. Then we shall say that ρ\rho is Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate if, for an arbitrary continuous automorphism α\alpha of GkG_{k}, the composite ρ∘α:Gk→Autℚp⁡(V)\rho\circ\alpha\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(V) is Hodge-Tate.

Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of the ring of integers 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} of kk. In the remainder of the present introduction, we write ρk,π:Gk→Autℚp⁡(k+)\rho_{k,\pi}\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(k_{+}) for the continuous pp-adic representation obtained by forming the composite

Gk→χk,π𝒪k×↪Autℚp​(k+),\displaystyle G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\chi_{k,\pi}}}{{\to}}\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(k_{+}),

where the first arrow is the Lubin-Tate character χk,π:Gk→𝒪k×\chi_{k,\pi}\colon G_{k}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times} [i.e., the continuous character determined by a Lubin-Tate formal group law over 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} associated to π\pi], and the second arrow is the natural inclusion.

It is natural to study which representations are Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate. The following theorem is a typical example motivated by this question:

Theorem B ([7], Theorem 3.3; [9], Theorem 1.9; [13], Theorem 4.4).

Let VV be a finite-dimensional ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-vector space and ρ:Gk→Autℚp⁡(V)\rho\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(V) a continuous pp-adic representation. Then the following assertions hold:

  1. (1)

    Suppose either that ρ\rho is one-dimensional or that ρ\rho is two-dimensional and reducible. Then ρ\rho is Hodge-Tate if and only if ρ\rho is Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate.

  2. (2)

    Suppose that p≥3p\geq 3 and that k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is a finite Galois extension of even degree. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. If ρ\rho is isomorphic to the continuous pp-adic representation ρk,π\rho_{k,\pi} of GkG_{k}, then ρ\rho is not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate.

  3. (3)

    Suppose that p=2p=2 and that kk contains a primitive 44-th root of unity. Suppose, moreover, that k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is an abelian extension. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. If ρ\rho is isomorphic to the continuous pp-adic representation ρk,π\rho_{k,\pi} of GkG_{k}, then ρ\rho is not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate.

Remark.

We give some remarks on Theorem B.

  1. (1)

    In the proof of Theorem B, (1), it is essential that the pp-adic cyclotomic character can be reconstructed from GkG_{k} in a group-theoretic manner. This is a significant difference between the pp-adic cyclotomic character and other Lubin-Tate characters.

  2. (2)

    In [7] and [9] [resp. [13]], Theorem B, (2) [resp. Theorem B, (3)] is not stated explicitly. However, the authors of [7] and [9] essentially established Theorem B, (2), while the author of [13] essentially established Theorem B, (3). Theorem B, (2) was first established in [7] for the case where k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is an abelian extension of even degree. In [7], by making use of the assumption that the extension is of even degree and abelian, the argument was reduced to the case where k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is a quadratic extension.

  3. (3)

    In [7] and [9] [resp. [13]], each of the authors constructed an explicit continuous automorphism φ\varphi of GkG_{k} such that ρk,π∘φ\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\varphi is not Hodge-Tate, in terms of the generators and relations established by Jannsen-Wingberg [cf. [12], Theorem 7.5.14] [resp. by Diekert [cf. [1], Theorem 3.1]].

In the present paper, we show the following theorem:

Theorem C (Theorem 3.5).

Suppose that k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is a nontrivial finite Galois extension and that either p≥3p\geq 3 or −1∈k\sqrt{-1}\in k. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer. Endow Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) with its natural profinite topology and its [normalized] Haar measure. Then the subset

Eout=def{α∈Out⁡(Gk)|ρk,π∘α~​ is Hodge-Tate},\displaystyle E_{\rm out}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\left\{\alpha\in\Out(G_{k})\ \middle|\ \rho_{k,\pi}\circ\widetilde{\alpha}\text{ is Hodge-Tate}\right\},

where α~\widetilde{\alpha} denotes an arbitrary representative of α\alpha in Aut⁡(Gk)\Aut(G_{k}), is contained in a closed subgroup of Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) of Haar measure zero.

In other words, under the assumptions of Theorem C, a Lubin-Tate representation of GkG_{k} fails to be Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate in a strong sense: for almost all outer automorphisms α\alpha of GkG_{k}, the representation obtained by composing it with α\alpha is not Hodge-Tate.

In particular, we obtain the following theorem, which is a generalization of Theorem B, (2) and (3), above:

Theorem D (Corollary 3.6).

Suppose that k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is a nontrivial finite Galois extension and that either p≥3p\geq 3 or −1∈k\sqrt{-1}\in k. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. Then the continuous pp-adic representation ρk,π:Gk→Autℚp⁡(k+)\rho_{k,\pi}\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(k_{+}) is not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate.

Remark.

We give some remarks on Theorem D.

  1. (1)

    In the case where p≥3p\geq 3, the novelty of Theorem D lies in the odd-degree cases [cf. Theorem B, (2)], although the argument proving the stronger Theorem C treats both odd and even degrees. From that point of view, the proof of Theorem C in the present paper is more uniform than the proofs of Theorem B, (2), in [7] and [9]. Theorem D also extends the previously known result by removing the assumption that k/ℚ2k/\mathbb{Q}_{2} is abelian [cf. Theorem B, (3)], under the assumption that k/ℚ2k/\mathbb{Q}_{2} is Galois and −1∈k\sqrt{-1}\in k.

  2. (2)

    In the proof of Theorem D, we do not give an explicit continuous automorphism φ\varphi of GkG_{k} such that ρk,π∘φ\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\varphi is not Hodge-Tate. Thus, when [k:ℚp][k:\mathbb{Q}_{p}] is even, both the method based on explicit generators and relations employed in [7], [9], and [13] [cf. Remark on Theorem B, (3)] and the method in the present paper have their own advantages and disadvantages.

At the end of the Introduction, we describe the outline of the proof of Theorem C. Let α\alpha be a continuous automorphism of GkG_{k}. We write α+\alpha_{+} for the automorphism of the ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-vector space k+k_{+} induced by the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithms [cf. [6], Definition 3.10, (vi); [6], Proposition 3.11, (iv); [8], Lemma 1.2; see also the discussion entitled “Groups of MLF-type” in the section on notational conventions below]. Then the main new ingredient in the proof is a characterization of the Hodge-Tate-ness of ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha in terms of the induced automorphism α+\alpha_{+}. More precisely, we show the following theorem:

Theorem E (Theorem 2.6).

Suppose that k/ℚpk/\mathbb{Q}_{p} is a finite Galois extension. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} and α\alpha a continuous automorphism of GkG_{k}. Then the continuous pp-adic representation ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha is Hodge-Tate if and only if there exists an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/ℚp)\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb{Q}_{p}) such that

α+=∑σ∈Gal⁡(k/ℚp)iσ⋅σ.\displaystyle\alpha_{+}=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb{Q}_{p})}i_{\sigma}\cdot\sigma.

In particular, if ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha is Hodge-Tate, then α+∈ℚp​[Gal⁡(k/ℚp)]×\alpha_{+}\in\mathbb{Q}_{p}[\operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb{Q}_{p})]^{\times}.

Thus, by means of the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithms, the pp-adic Hodge-theoretic condition that ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha be Hodge-Tate is translated into a linear-algebraic condition on the automorphism of k+k_{+} induced by α\alpha. We then combine this characterization with the theory of mapping class groups and the theory of pp-adic Lie groups to prove Theorem C.

0. Notational conventions

Profinite groups. Let GG be a profinite group and α\alpha a continuous automorphism of the topological group GG. Then we shall write GabG^{\ab} for the abelianization of GG [i.e., the quotient of GG by the closure of the commutator subgroup of GG] and αab\alpha^{\mathrm{ab}} for the continuous automorphism of the topological group GabG^{\mathrm{ab}} induced by α\alpha via the functoriality of abelianization.

Rings. In the present paper, every “ring” is assumed to be unital and associative. If RR is a ring, then we shall write R+R_{+} for the underlying additive group of RR and R×⊂RR^{\times}\subset R for the multiplicative group of units of RR.

Mixed-characteristic local fields. We shall refer to a field isomorphic to a finite extension of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, for some prime number pp, as an MLF. Here, “MLF” is to be understood as an abbreviation for “mixed-characteristic local field”. We recall that the valuation-theoretic structure of a finite extension of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} is functorially determined by its field structure. Thus, for an MLF kk, the usual valuation-theoretic objects are determined by the field structure of kk. Let kk be an MLF and k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk. Then we shall write

  • •

    𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} for the ring of integers of kk,

  • •

    𝔪k⊂𝒪k\mathfrak{m}_{k}\subset\mathcal{O}_{k} for the maximal ideal of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k},

  • •

    k¯=def𝒪k/𝔪k\underline{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\mathcal{O}_{k}/\mathfrak{m}_{k} for the residue field of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k},

  • •

    k(d=1)⊂kk^{(d=1)}\subset k for the [uniquely determined] minimal MLF contained in kk,

  • •

    pkp_{k} for the residue characteristic of kk,

  • •

    dk=def[k:k(d=1)]d_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}[k\colon k^{(d=1)}] for the degree of the finite extension k/k(d=1)k/k^{(d=1)},

  • •

    fk=def[k¯:k¯(d=1)]f_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}[\underline{k}\colon\underline{k}^{(d=1)}] for the degree of the finite extension k¯/k¯(d=1)\underline{k}/\underline{k}^{(d=1)} [where we write k¯(d=1)\underline{k}^{(d=1)} for the residue field of the ring of integers of the MLF k(d=1)k^{(d=1)}],

  • •

    aka_{k} for the largest nonnegative integer such that kk contains a primitive pkakp_{k}^{a_{k}}-th root of unity,

  • •

    Gk=defGal⁡(k¯/k)G_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\Gal(\overline{k}/k) for the absolute Galois group of kk determined by the algebraic closure k¯\overline{k},

  • •

    Ik⊂GkI_{k}\subset G_{k} for the inertia subgroup of GkG_{k},

  • •

    Pk⊂IkP_{k}\subset I_{k} for the wild inertia subgroup of GkG_{k},

  • •

    logk:𝒪k×→k+\log_{k}\colon\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\to k_{+} for the pkp_{k}-adic logarithm,

  • •

    k×^\widehat{k^{\times}} for the profinite completion of the multiplicative group k×k^{\times} of kk, and

  • •

    reck:k×^⟶∼Gkab\rec_{k}\colon\widehat{k^{\times}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}G_{k}^{\ab} for the isomorphism induced by the reciprocity homomorphism k×↪Gkabk^{\times}\hookrightarrow G_{k}^{\ab} in local class field theory.

Groups of MLF-type. We shall refer to a topological group isomorphic to the absolute Galois group of an MLF as a group of MLF-type.

Let us recall [cf. [6], Definition 3.5; [6], Proposition 3.6; [6], Definition 3.10; [6], Proposition 3.11; [5], Definition 2.4, (ii)\rm(\hskip 0.80002ptii\hskip 0.80002pt); [5], Proposition 2.5, (i)\rm(\hskip 0.80002pti\hskip 0.80002pt)] that there exist functorial group-theoretic algorithms for constructing, from a group of MLF-type GG,

  • •

    a prime number p⁡(G)p(G),

  • •

    positive integers d⁡(G)d(G), f⁡(G)f(G),

  • •

    a nonnegative integer a⁡(G)a(G),

  • •

    subgroups P⁡(G)⊂I⁡(G)⊂GP(G)\subset I(G)\subset G of GG,

  • •

    subgroups 𝒪×​(G)⊂k×​(G)⊂Gab\mathcal{O}^{\times}(G)\subset k^{\times}(G)\subset G^{\ab}, whose final inclusion k×​(G)⊂Gabk^{\times}(G)\subset G^{\ab} we denote by recG\rec_{G}, and

  • •

    a topological group k+​(G)k_{+}(G),

which “correspond” to

  • •

    the prime number pkp_{k},

  • •

    the positive integers dkd_{k}, fkf_{k},

  • •

    the nonnegative integer aka_{k},

  • •

    the subgroups Pk⊂Ik⊂GkP_{k}\subset I_{k}\subset G_{k} of GkG_{k},

  • •

    the subgroups 𝒪k×⊂k×↪reckGkab\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\subset k^{\times}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rec_{k}}}{{\hookrightarrow}}G_{k}^{\ab}, and

  • •

    the topological group k+k_{+},

respectively.

By the functoriality of the algorithms, we have natural homomorphisms

Aut⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k×​(G)),Aut⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k+​(G)).\displaystyle\Aut(G)\to\Aut(k^{\times}(G)),\ \ \ \Aut(G)\to\Aut(k_{+}(G)).

Since the automorphism of GabG^{\ab} induced by an inner automorphism of GG is trivial, it follows from the constructions of k×​(G)k^{\times}(G) and k+​(G)k_{+}(G) that the automorphisms of k×​(G)k^{\times}(G) and k+​(G)k_{+}(G) induced by an inner automorphism of GG are trivial. Thus, the above two homomorphisms determine group homomorphisms

Out⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k×​(G)),Out⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k+​(G)).\displaystyle\Out(G)\to\Aut(k^{\times}(G)),\ \ \ \Out(G)\to\Aut(k_{+}(G)).

Let α\alpha be an element of Out⁡(G)\Out(G). We write α×\alpha^{\times} [resp. α+\alpha_{+}] for the image of α\alpha by this homomorphism Out⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k×​(G))\Out(G)\to\Aut(k^{\times}(G)) [resp. Out⁡(G)→Aut⁡(k+​(G))\Out(G)\to\Aut(k_{+}(G))]. In the present paper, we call α×\alpha^{\times} and α+\alpha_{+} the automorphisms induced from α\alpha by the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithms.

Let kk be an MLF, k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk, and α\alpha an element of Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}). By abuse of notation, we shall denote by α+:k+⟶∼k+\alpha_{+}\colon k_{+}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k_{+}, α×:k×⟶∼k×\alpha^{\times}\colon k^{\times}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k^{\times} the respective images of α+:k+​(Gk)⟶∼k+​(Gk)\alpha_{+}\colon k_{+}(G_{k})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k_{+}(G_{k}), α×:k×​(Gk)⟶∼k×​(Gk)\alpha^{\times}\colon k^{\times}(G_{k})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k^{\times}(G_{k}) by the isomorphisms Aut⁡(k+​(Gk))⟶∼Aut⁡(k+)\Aut(k_{+}(G_{k}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Aut(k_{+}), Aut⁡(k×​(Gk))⟶∼Aut⁡(k×)\Aut(k^{\times}(G_{k}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Aut(k^{\times}) induced by the isomorphisms k+⟶∼k+​(Gk)k_{+}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k_{+}(G_{k}), k×⟶∼k×​(Gk)k^{\times}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k^{\times}(G_{k}) of [6], Proposition 3.11, (i)\rm(\hskip 1.79993pti\hskip 1.79993pt), (iv)\rm(i\hskip-0.80002ptv\hskip-0.59998pt).

1. Representation induced by the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithm

In the present section, we recall, for the convenience of the reader, various notions introduced in [9] and [13], as well as some relevant results. Let kk be an MLF, k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk, and GG a group of MLF-type.

Remark 1.1.

It follows immediately from the various definitions involved that if pk=2p_{k}=2, then ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2 if and only if −1∈k\sqrt{-1}\in k. Thus, if p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2, then the condition a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2 that appears frequently in the following discussion is precisely the group-theoretic condition corresponding to the existence of a primitive 4-th root of unity.

Theorem 1.2.

Write ϖ\varpi for the unique element of ℤ^=∏ℓℤℓ\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}=\prod_{\ell}\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} whose image in ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} is given by 11 if ℓ=p⁡(G)\ell=p(G) [resp. by 00 if ℓ≠p⁡(G)\ell\neq p(G)]. Suppose that either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2. Then there exist σ\sigma, τ\tau, x0,…,xd⁡(G)∈Gx_{0},\ldots,x_{d(G)}\in G, positive integers ss, tt, uu, and an element x1′∈⟨σ,τ,x1⟩¯x_{1}^{\prime}\in\overline{\langle\sigma,\tau,x_{1}\rangle}, where “⟨S⟩¯\overline{\langle S\rangle}” denotes the closed subgroup of GG topologically generated by “SS”, such that the following conditions hold:

  1. (0)

    We have

    t​∑j=1p⁡(G)−1uj≠p⁡(G)−1.\displaystyle t\sum_{j=1}^{p(G)-1}u^{j}\neq p(G)-1.
  2. (1)

    The profinite group GG is presented as the profinite group topologically generated by σ\sigma, τ\tau, x0,…,xd⁡(G)∈Gx_{0},\ldots,x_{d(G)}\in G and subject to the relations described in the conditions (2), (3), and (4) below.

  3. (2)

    The closed normal subgroup P⁡(G)P(G) of GG is pro-p⁡(G)p(G) and topologically normally generated by x0,…,xd⁡(G)x_{0},\ldots,x_{d(G)}.

  4. (3)

    The elements σ\sigma, τ\tau satisfy the relation σ​τ​σ−1=τp​(G)f⁡(G)\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\tau^{p(G)^{f(G)}}.

  5. (4)

    The generators satisfy one further relation:

    1. (a)

      for even d⁡(G)d(G),

      σx0σ−1=(∏j=1p⁡(G)−1x0up⁡(G)−jτ)ϖ​tp⁡(G)−1x1p​(G)s[x1,x2][x3,x4]⋯[xd⁡(G)−1,xd⁡(G)];\displaystyle\sigma x_{0}\sigma^{-1}=\Biggl(\prod_{j=1}^{p(G)-1}x_{0}^{u^{p(G)-j}}\tau\Biggr)^{\frac{\varpi t}{p(G)-1}}x_{1}^{p(G)^{s}}[x_{1},x_{2}][x_{3},x_{4}]\cdots[x_{d(G)-1},x_{d(G)}];

      for odd d⁡(G)d(G),

      σx0σ−1=(∏j=1p⁡(G)−1x0up⁡(G)−jτ)ϖ​tp⁡(G)−1x1p​(G)s[x1,x1′][x2,x3]⋯[xd⁡(G)−1,xd⁡(G)].\displaystyle\sigma x_{0}\sigma^{-1}=\Biggl(\prod_{j=1}^{p(G)-1}x_{0}^{u^{p(G)-j}}\tau\Biggr)^{\frac{\varpi t}{p(G)-1}}x_{1}^{p(G)^{s}}[x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime}][x_{2},x_{3}]\cdots[x_{d(G)-1},x_{d(G)}].
Proof.

When p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3, this assertion follows from [12], Theorem 7.5.14, together with [6], Proposition 3.6. When p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2 and a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2, this assertion follows, in light of Remark 1.1, from [1], Theorem 3.1, together with [6], Proposition 3.6. See also [8], Proposition 1.1 [when p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3], and [13], Proposition 1.1 [when p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2 and a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2]. ∎

In the remainder of the present paper, we apply the notational conventions introduced in the statement of Theorem 1.2 whenever either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2. Moreover, if p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2, then, for each i=1,2,…,d⁡(G)i=1,2,\ldots,d(G), write yi∈k+​(G)y_{i}\in k_{+}(G) for the image of xix_{i} in k+​(G)k_{+}(G) by the composite P⁡(G)↪I⁡(G)→𝒪×​(G)→k+​(G)P(G)\hookrightarrow I(G)\to\mathcal{O}^{\times}(G)\to k_{+}(G) [cf. conditions (1), (2) of Theorem 1.2; [6], Definition 3.10, (i)\rm(\hskip 1.79993pti\hskip 1.79993pt), (ii)\rm(\hskip 0.80002ptii\hskip 0.80002pt), (vi)\rm(\hskip 0.59998ptvi\hskip 0.59998pt)].

We recall that the topological group k+​(G)k_{+}(G) has a natural structure of a ℚp⁡(G)\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}-vector space of dimension d⁡(G)d(G) [cf. [8], Lemma 1.2; [13], Lemma 1.2] and that, for any continuous automorphism α\alpha of GG, the induced automorphism α+\alpha_{+} of k+​(G)k_{+}(G) is an automorphism of ℚp⁡(G)\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}-vector spaces.

Lemma 1.3.

Suppose that d⁡(G)>1d(G)>1 and that either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2. Then the d⁡(G)d(G) elements y1,…,yd⁡(G)y_{1},\ldots,y_{d(G)} defined in the discussion following Theorem 1.2 form a basis of the ℚp⁡(G)\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}-vector space k+​(G)k_{+}(G).

Proof.

When p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3, this assertion is none other than [8], Lemma 1.3. When p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2 and a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2, this assertion is none other than [13], Lemma 1.3. ∎

One verifies easily that the isomorphism of topological groups k+​(Gk)⟶∼k+k_{+}(G_{k})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k_{+} of [6], Proposition 3.11, (iv)\rm(i\hskip-0.80002ptv\hskip-0.59998pt), is also an isomorphism of ℚpk\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}-vector spaces [where we recall that pk=p⁡(Gk)p_{k}=p(G_{k})]. By abuse of notation, if dk>1d_{k}>1 and either pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3 or ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2, then, for each integer ii satisfying 1≤i≤dk1\leq i\leq d_{k}, we write yi∈k+y_{i}\in k_{+} for the image of yi∈k+​(Gk)y_{i}\in k_{+}(G_{k}) by the isomorphism k+​(Gk)⟶∼k+k_{+}(G_{k})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}k_{+} of [6], Proposition 3.11, (iv)\rm(i\hskip-0.80002ptv\hskip-0.59998pt).

In the remainder of the present paper, if d⁡(G)>1d(G)>1 [resp. dk>1d_{k}>1], and either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 [resp. pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3] or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2 [resp. ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2], then we equip k+​(G)k_{+}(G) [resp. k+k_{+}] with this basis, which allows us to identify Autℚp⁡(G)⁡(k+​(G))\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}}(k_{+}(G)) [resp. Autℚpk⁡(k+)\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})] with GLd⁡(G)⁡(ℚp⁡(G))\GL_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) [resp. GLdk⁡(ℚpk)\GL_{d_{k}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}})]. We equip GLd⁡(G)⁡(ℚp⁡(G))\GL_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) [resp. GLdk⁡(ℚpk)\GL_{d_{k}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}})] with the natural p⁡(G)p(G)-adic [resp. pkp_{k}-adic] Lie group structure.

Definition 1.4.

We shall say that the MLF kk is absolutely Galois if the extension k/k(d=1)k/k^{(d=1)} is a Galois extension.

Remark 1.5.

Since the elements of Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)}), regarded as a subset of Endℚpk⁡(k+)\End_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}), are linearly independent over ℚpk\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}} [cf. [10], Chapter VI\rm VI, §4, Theorem 4.1], the natural map

ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]→Endℚpk⁡(k+)\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]\to\End_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})

is injective. In light of this observation, we shall regard ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})] as a sub-ℚpk\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}-algebra of Endℚpk⁡(k+)\End_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}) via this injective homomorphism in the following discussion.

In this context, we also observe that

Indeed, the inclusion Autℚpk⁡(k+)∩ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]⊃ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]×\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})\cap\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]\supset\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]^{\times} is trivial. Next, we prove the reverse inclusion. Let β∈Autℚpk⁡(k+)∩ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]\beta\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})\cap\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\operatorname{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})] be an arbitrary element, and write

Xn+a1​Xn−1+⋯+an−1​X+an\displaystyle X^{n}+a_{1}X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}X+a_{n}

for the minimal polynomial of β\beta over ℚpk\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}. Since β∈Autℚpk⁡(k+)\beta\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}), we have an≠0a_{n}\neq 0. Thus, we have

which proves the desired inclusion.

Next, we review the profinite group structure of Out⁡(G)\Out(G). It follows from [12], Theorem 7.4.1, and [14], Proposition 4.4.3, that Out⁡(G)\Out(G) has a natural profinite group structure. In the remainder of the present paper, we endow Out⁡(G)\Out(G) with this profinite group structure.

In the remainder of the present section, we assume that d⁡(G)>1d(G)>1 [resp. dk>1d_{k}>1] and either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 [resp. pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3] or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2 [resp. ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2].

Lemma 1.6.

The action Out​(G)↷k+​(G)\mathrm{Out}(G)\curvearrowright k_{+}(G) which is defined via the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithm is continuous. In particular, the induced map

Φ:Out⁡(G)→Autℚp⁡(G)⁡(k+​(G))⟶∼GLd⁡(G)​(ℚp⁡(G))\displaystyle\Phi\colon\Out(G)\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}}(k_{+}(G))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{GL}_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)})

is continuous and closed.

Proof.

When p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3, this assertion is none other than [9], Lemma 2.13. When p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2 and a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2, this assertion follows, in light of Theorem 1.2 and the various definitions involved, by a similar argument to the argument applied in the proof of [9], Lemma 2.13. ∎

Lemma 1.7.

The image of the homomorphism Φ\Phi of Lemma 1.6 has a natural p⁡(G)p(G)-adic Lie group structure.

Proof.

This assertion follows immediately from Lemma 1.6, together with [2], Theorem 9.6. ∎

Lemma 1.8.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF. We shall write ZZ for the image of ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]×\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})]^{\times} in GLdk​(ℚpk)\mathrm{GL}_{d_{k}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}) via the isomorphism Autℚpk⁡(k+)⟶∼GLdk​(ℚpk)\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{GL}_{d_{k}}(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}) determined by the basis y1,…,ydky_{1},\ldots,y_{d_{k}} of k+k_{+}. Then the following assertions hold:

Assertion (1) follows immediately from the [easily verified] fact that ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]×⊂Autℚpk⁡(k+)\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]^{\times}\subset\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}) is closed [cf. Remark 1.5], together with [2], Theorem 9.6.

Assertion (2) follows immediately from Remark 1.5 and the easily verified fact that

dim(ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))])=dk,\displaystyle\dim(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})])=d_{k},

where we write dim(ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))])\dim(\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]) for the dimension of ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})] as a pkp_{k}-adic Lie group. This completes the proof of Lemma 1.8. ∎

2. Classification of abelian Hodge-Tate representations

In the present section, we review a classification theorem of abelian Hodge-Tate representations. Moreover, by combining the classification of abelian Hodge-Tate representations with the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithm, we obtain Theorem 2.6, which will provide the key observation for the proof of the main theorem of the present paper. Let kk be an MLF and k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk.

In the present section, we do not make use of the presentation in terms of generators and relations of groups of MLF-type introduced in Theorem 1.2. Thus, even when pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3 or ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2, we do not fix generators of GkG_{k} satisfying the conditions of Theorem 1.2.

Definition 2.1.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF [cf. Definition 1.4]. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} and σ\sigma an element of Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)}). Then we shall write

χπ,σ:Gkab→reck−1k×^↠𝒪k×→σ𝒪k×,\displaystyle\chi_{\pi,\sigma}\colon G_{k}^{\ab}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rec_{k}^{-1}}}{{\to}}\widehat{k^{\times}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma}}{{\to}}\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times},

where the second arrow is the projection determined by π\pi.

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} and ϕ:Gkab→𝒪k×\phi\colon G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times} a continuous homomorphism. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    The continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation obtained by forming the composite

    Gk↠Gkab→ϕ𝒪k×↪Autℚpk​(k+)\displaystyle G_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\to}}\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+})

    — where the first arrow is the natural surjective continuous homomorphism, and the third arrow is the natural inclusion — is Hodge-Tate.

  2. (2)

    There exist an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) and an open subgroup J⊂IkJ\subset I_{k} such that

    • •

      the restriction to JJ of the composite of the natural surjective continuous homomorphism Gk↠GkabG_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}} and the given homomorphism ϕ:Gkab→𝒪k×\phi\colon G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}

    coincides with

    • •

      the restriction to JJ of the composite of the natural surjective continuous homomorphism Gk↠GkabG_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}} and the homomorphism

      ∏σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))χπ,σiσ:Gkab→𝒪k×.\displaystyle\prod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})}\chi_{\pi,\sigma}^{i_{\sigma}}\colon G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}.
Proof.

This assertion follows from the classification of abelian Hodge-Tate representations due to Serre [cf. [15], Chapter III\rm I\hskip-1.49994ptI\hskip-1.49994ptI, §A.5, Corollary]. See [7], Lemma 1.8, for a formulation adapted to the present setting. ∎

Definition 2.3.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. Then we write ρk,π:Gk→Autℚpk​(k+)\rho_{k,\pi}\colon G_{k}\to\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}) for the continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation of GkG_{k} obtained by forming the composite

Gk↠Gkab→χπ,idk𝒪k×↪Autℚpk​(k+),\displaystyle G_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\chi_{\pi,\id_{k}}}}{{\to}}\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(k_{+}),

where the first arrow is the natural surjective continuous homomorphism, and the third arrow is the natural inclusion.

Remark 2.4.

It follows from [15], Chapter III\rm I\hskip-1.49994ptI\hskip-1.49994ptI, §A.4, Proposition 4, that, up to taking the dual, the pkp_{k}-adic representation ρk,π\rho_{k,\pi} is isomorphic to the continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation determined by a Lubin-Tate character [i.e., a continuous character determined by a Lubin-Tate formal group over 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}]. Here, whether or not the dual occurs depends on the normalization of local reciprocity [equivalently, on the choice between arithmetic and geometric Frobenius]. Thus, it follows from [3], Theorem 6.2, (i)(\rm i), that the continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation ρk,π\rho_{k,\pi} is crystalline [hence also Hodge-Tate].

Remark 2.5.

It follows from [15], Chapter III\rm I\hskip-1.49994ptI\hskip-1.49994ptI, §A.1, Corollary 2, that the Hodge-Tate-ness of continuous pkp_{k}-adic representations of GkG_{k} is independent of the choice of representatives of an inertial equivalence class [cf., e.g., [4], Definition 1.2, (i)\rm(\hskip 1.79993pti\hskip 1.79993pt)], where we recall that, for a finite-dimensional ℚpk\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}-vector space VV, two representations ρ,ρ′:Gk→Autℚpk⁡(V)\rho,\rho^{\prime}\colon G_{k}\to\Aut_{\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}}(V) are referred to as inertially equivalent if there exists an open subgroup J⊂IkJ\subset I_{k} of IkI_{k} such that ρ|J=ρ′|J\rho|_{J}=\rho^{\prime}|_{J}. Moreover, one verifies easily that the inertial equivalence class of χπ,idk\chi_{\pi,\id_{k}} is independent of the choice of a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. Thus, the choice of a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} is inessential for the discussion that follows.

The following theorem constitutes the main novelty of the present paper:

Theorem 2.6.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} and α\alpha a continuous automorphism of GkG_{k}. Then the following assertions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    The continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha is Hodge-Tate.

  2. (2)

    There exists an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) such that

    α+=∑σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))iσ⋅σ.\displaystyle\alpha_{+}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})}i_{\sigma}\cdot\sigma.

In particular, if ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha is Hodge-Tate, then α+∈ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]×\alpha_{+}\in\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]^{\times} [cf. Remark 1.5].

Proof.

First, we show (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2). Suppose that ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha is Hodge-Tate. Then it follows from Theorem 2.2 that there exist an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) and an open subgroup J⊂IkJ\subset I_{k} such that

  • •

    the restriction to JJ of the composite of the natural surjective continuous homomorphism Gk↠GkabG_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}} and the homomorphism

    χπ,idk∘αab:Gkab→𝒪k×\displaystyle\chi_{\pi,\id_{k}}\circ\alpha^{\mathrm{ab}}\colon G_{k}^{\ab}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}

coincides with

  • •

    the restriction to JJ of the composite of the natural surjective continuous homomorphism Gk↠GkabG_{k}\twoheadrightarrow G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}} and the homomorphism

    ∏σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))χπ,σiσ:Gkab→𝒪k×.\displaystyle\prod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})}\chi_{\pi,\sigma}^{i_{\sigma}}\colon G_{k}^{\mathrm{ab}}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}.

Thus, it follows from the definition of α×\alpha^{\times} that there exist an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) and an open subgroup U⊂𝒪k×U\subset\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times} such that

  • •

    the restriction to UU of the homomorphism

    α×:𝒪k×→𝒪k×\displaystyle\alpha^{\times}\colon\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}

coincides with

  • •

    the restriction to UU of the homomorphism

    ∏σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))σiσ:𝒪k×→𝒪k×,\displaystyle\prod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})}\sigma_{i_{\sigma}}\colon\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times},

where we write σiσ\sigma_{i_{\sigma}} for the endomorphism of 𝒪k×\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times} defined by x↦σ​(x)iσx\mapsto\sigma(x)^{i_{\sigma}}. Let us recall that it follows from the definition of α+\alpha_{+} and [6], Proposition 3.11, (iv)\rm(i\hskip-0.80002ptv\hskip-0.59998pt), that the following diagram commutes:

Thus, it follows from [11], Lemma 4.1, together with the commutativity of the diagram above, that for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) there exists an integer iσi_{\sigma} such that

α+=∑σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))iσ⋅σ.\displaystyle\alpha_{+}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)})}i_{\sigma}\cdot\sigma.

This completes the proof of the implication (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2).

Next, we show (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1). It is well-known that the pkp_{k}-adic logarithm is injective on a sufficiently small open subgroup of 𝒪k×\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}. Thus, in light of the commutative diagram above, the assumption (2) implies that there exist an open subgroup U⊂𝒪k×U\subset\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times} and an integer iσi_{\sigma} for each σ∈Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(k/k^{(d=1)}) such that

  • •

    the restriction to UU of the homomorphism

    α×:𝒪k×→𝒪k×\displaystyle\alpha^{\times}\colon\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}\to\mathcal{O}_{k}^{\times}

coincides with

Remark 2.7.

The significance of this theorem lies in the fact that, by means of the mono-anabelian reconstruction algorithm, the Hodge-Tate-ness of ρk,π∘α\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\alpha can be reduced to a linear-algebraic condition, which can then be studied by pkp_{k}-adic Lie-theoretic methods. If a similar result could be formulated for more general Hodge-Tate representations, it might provide a means of investigating whether such representations are Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate.

3. Mapping class groups and the proof of the main theorem

In the present section, we prove the main theorem of the present paper by combining Theorem 2.6 with certain “mapping class group and pp-adic Lie group techniques” developed in [9].

Let kk be an MLF, k¯\overline{k} an algebraic closure of kk, and GG a group of MLF-type. Let us recall that Out⁡(G)\Out(G) [resp. Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k})] has been endowed with its natural profinite group structure.

We assume that d⁡(G)>1d(G)>1 [resp. dk>1d_{k}>1] and either p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 [resp. pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3] or a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2 [resp. ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2]. Let us recall that, in this situation, generators of GG [resp. GkG_{k}] satisfying Theorem 1.2, as well as the basis y1,…,yd⁡(G)y_{1},\ldots,y_{d(G)} [resp. y1,…,ydky_{1},\ldots,y_{d_{k}}] of k+​(G)k_{+}(G) [resp. k+k_{+}] determined by these generators, have been fixed.

First, we review the subgroup of Out⁡(G)\mathrm{Out}(G) that corresponds to a “mapping class group” introduced in the discussion following [9], Lemma 2.15.

Remark 3.1.

In [9], it is assumed that p⁡(G)≥3p(G)\geq 3 [resp. pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3]. We note, however, that the mapping class group construction developed there depends only on the existence of a presentation in terms of generators and relations of “Jannsen-Wingberg-Diekert type”. Thus, it follows from Theorem 1.2 that the same construction and arguments apply verbatim when p⁡(G)=2p(G)=2 [resp. pk=2p_{k}=2] and a⁡(G)≥2a(G)\geq 2 [resp. ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2].

Definition 3.2.

Suppose that d⁡(G)≥3d(G)\geq 3.

  1. (1)

    We shall write

    Also, recall that there exists [cf. the discussion following [9], Lemma 2.15] a map

    ρ:Mod⁡(S∖{P})→Out⁡(G),\displaystyle\rho\colon\Mod(S\setminus\{P\})\to\Out(G),

    which is not necessarily a homomorphism of groups, such that the following diagram is commutative:

    where the lower horizontal arrow is the surjective homomorphism discussed in [9], Theorem 2.17. We fix such a ρ\rho. Then we shall write D⊂Out⁡(G)D\subset\Out(G) for the closed subgroup of Out⁡(G)\Out(G) that is topologically generated by the image of ρ\rho.

In the remainder of the present paper, whenever d⁡(G)≥3d(G)\geq 3, we continue to regard Sp2​g​(ℤp⁡(G))\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p(G)}) as a subgroup of GLd⁡(G)⁡(ℚp⁡(G))\GL_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) via the above injective group homomorphism. Also, in what follows, for a p⁡(G)p(G)-adic [pkp_{k}-adic] Lie group XX, we write dim(X)\dim(X) for the dimension of XX as a p⁡(G)p(G)-adic [pkp_{k}-adic] Lie group.

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose that d⁡(G)≥3d(G)\geq 3. Then the image of the homomorphism Φ:Out⁡(G)→GLd⁡(G)​(ℚp⁡(G))\Phi\colon\Out(G)\to\mathrm{GL}_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) of Lemma 1.6 contains Sp2​g​(ℤp⁡(G))\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p(G)}). In particular, we have dim(Im⁡(Φ))≥2​g2+g\dim(\mathrm{Im}(\Phi))\geq 2g^{2}+g.

Proof.

It follows immediately from Lemma 1.6, the commutative diagram above, and the fact that the topological closure of Sp2​g​(ℤ)\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}) in GLd⁡(G)⁡(ℚp⁡(G))\GL_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) is Sp2​g​(ℤp⁡(G))⊂GLd⁡(G)⁡(ℚp⁡(G))\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p(G)})\subset\GL_{d(G)}(\mathbb{Q}_{p(G)}) that Φ⁡(D)⊃Sp2​g​(ℤp⁡(G))\Phi(D)\supset\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p(G)}). This completes the proof of the first assertion. The second assertion follows immediately from the first assertion, together with the well-known equality dim(Sp2​g​(ℤp⁡(G)))=2​g2+g\dim(\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p(G)}))=2g^{2}+g. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Let nn be a positive integer. Then the profinite group Sp2​n​(ℤpk)\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{Z}_{p_{k}}) is not a virtually abelian profinite group, i.e., has no abelian open subgroup.

Proof.

When pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3, this assertion is none other than [9], Lemma 2.15. Although pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3 is assumed in [9], its proof applies verbatim to pk=2p_{k}=2. This completes the proof of Lemma 3.4. ∎

With the above preparations, we now prove the main theorem of the present paper.

Theorem 3.5.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF, that either pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3 or ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2, and that dk>1d_{k}>1. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. We endow the profinite group Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) with its [normalized] Haar measure. Then the subset

Eout=def{α∈Out⁡(Gk)|ρk,π∘α~​ is Hodge-Tate},\displaystyle E_{\rm out}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\left\{\alpha\in\Out(G_{k})\ \middle|\ \rho_{k,\pi}\circ\widetilde{\alpha}\text{ is Hodge-Tate}\right\},

where α~\widetilde{\alpha} denotes an arbitrary representative of α\alpha in Aut⁡(Gk)\Aut(G_{k}), is contained in a closed subgroup of Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) of Haar measure zero.

Proof.

First, we note that the condition appearing in the definition of EoutE_{\rm out} is independent of the choice of the representative α~\widetilde{\alpha}. Indeed, precomposition by an inner automorphism changes a representation only by an isomorphism.

Write I=defIm⁡(Φ)I\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\mathrm{Im}(\Phi), and K=defI∩ZK\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}I\cap Z. Then it follows from Theorem 2.6 that if ρk,π∘α~\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\widetilde{\alpha} is Hodge-Tate, then Φ⁡(α)∈Z\Phi(\alpha)\in Z. Consequently, we obtain

Eout⊂Φ−1​(K).\displaystyle E_{\rm out}\subset\Phi^{-1}(K).

Next, we prove the following claim:

Claim.

The closed subgroup K⊂IK\subset I is not open in II. Equivalently, the closed subgroup K⊂IK\subset I is not of finite index in II.

We first consider the case where dk≥5d_{k}\geq 5. Let g=defg⁡(Gk)(≥2)g\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}g(G_{k})(\geq 2). Then it follows from Lemma 3.3 that dim(I)≥2​g2+g\dim(I)\geq 2g^{2}+g. On the other hand, it follows from Lemma 1.8 that dim(K)≤dim(Z)≤dk\dim(K)\leq\dim(Z)\leq d_{k}. If dkd_{k} is odd, then dk=2​g+1d_{k}=2g+1, whereas if dkd_{k} is even, then dk=2​g+2d_{k}=2g+2. Thus, the inequalities dk≤2​g+2<2​g2+gd_{k}\leq 2g+2<2g^{2}+g [cf. the condition that g≥2g\geq 2]. In particular, it follows that dim(K)<dim(I)\dim(K)<\dim(I). Thus, the closed subgroup K⊂IK\subset I cannot be open in II.

We next consider the case where dk=3,4d_{k}=3,4 [i.e., g=1g=1]. In either case, since every group of order 33 or 44 is abelian, the group Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)}) is abelian. Hence the algebra ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})] is commutative, so ZZ, and therefore KK, is abelian. On the other hand, it follows from Lemma 3.3 that Sp2​(ℤpk)⊂I\mathrm{Sp}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p_{k}})\subset I. If KK were open in II, then K∩Sp2​(ℤpk)K\cap\mathrm{Sp}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p_{k}}) would be an abelian open subgroup of Sp2​(ℤpk)\mathrm{Sp}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p_{k}}). This contradicts Lemma 3.4. Thus KK is not open in II also in this case.

It remains to consider the case where dk=2d_{k}=2. Write φ\varphi for the automorphism of GkG_{k} defined by

φ(σ)=σ,φ(τ)=τ,φ(x2)=x2x1,φ(xi)=xi(i≠2).\displaystyle\varphi(\sigma)=\sigma,\qquad\varphi(\tau)=\tau,\qquad\varphi(x_{2})=x_{2}x_{1},\qquad\varphi(x_{i})=x_{i}\quad(i\neq 2).

It follows from [8], Lemma 2.4 [when pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3], and [13], Lemma 2.3 [when pk=2p_{k}=2 and ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2], that, for every n∈ℤ∖{0}n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}, we have

(φn)+​((k(d=1))+)≠(k(d=1))+.\displaystyle(\varphi^{n})_{+}\bigl((k^{(d=1)})_{+}\bigr)\neq(k^{(d=1)})_{+}.

On the other hand, since the group Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)}) acts trivially on k(d=1)k^{(d=1)}, and the restriction to (k(d=1))+(k^{(d=1)})_{+} of an element of ℚpk​[Gal⁡(k/k(d=1))]×\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}[\Gal(k/k^{(d=1)})]^{\times} is multiplication by its augmentation, which belongs to ℚpk×\mathbb{Q}_{p_{k}}^{\times}, every element of ZZ preserves (k(d=1))+(k^{(d=1)})_{+}. Let φ¯\overline{\varphi} denote the image of φ\varphi in Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) and put c=defΦ⁡(φ¯)∈Ic\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\Phi(\overline{\varphi})\in I. The preceding observations imply that cn∉Zc^{n}\notin Z for all n∈ℤ∖{0}n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}. Suppose, for a contradiction, that KK is open in II, and write

C=def⟨c⟩¯⊂I.\displaystyle C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\overline{\langle c\rangle}\subset I.

Then C∩KC\cap K is an open subgroup of the profinite group CC, hence is of finite index in CC. In particular, it follows that there exists an integer m>0m>0 such that

cm∈C∩K⊂Z,\displaystyle c^{m}\in C\cap K\subset Z,

which contradicts the preceding assertion. Thus, the closed subgroup K⊂IK\subset I is not open in II also when dk=2d_{k}=2. We have therefore proved, in every case dk>1d_{k}>1, that the closed subgroup K⊂IK\subset I is not open [i.e., not of finite index]. This completes the proof of the above claim.

Since II is compact [i.e., of finite Haar measure], this readily implies that μI​(K)=0\mu_{I}(K)=0, where μI\mu_{I} is the normalized Haar measure of II.

Since Φ:Out⁡(Gk)↠I\Phi\colon\Out(G_{k})\twoheadrightarrow I is a continuous surjective homomorphism of compact groups, it follows from the uniqueness of normalized Haar measure that the pushforward of the normalized Haar measure μout\mu_{\mathrm{out}} on Out⁡(Gk)\Out(G_{k}) under Φ\Phi is the normalized Haar measure on II. Therefore, the equality

μout​(Φ−1​(K))=μI​(K)=0\displaystyle\mu_{\rm out}\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(K)\bigr)=\mu_{I}(K)=0

hold. Since Eout⊂Φ−1​(K)E_{\mathrm{out}}\subset\Phi^{-1}(K), this completes the proof of Theorem 3.5. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

Suppose that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF, that either pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3 or ak≥2a_{k}\geq 2, and that dk>1d_{k}>1. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. Then the continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation ρk,π\rho_{k,\pi} is not Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate [cf. Definition in Introduction].

Proof.

This assertion follows immediately from Theorem 3.5. ∎

Remark 3.7.

In [9], the author of the present paper proved the following assertion:

Suppose that pk≥3p_{k}\geq 3, that dkd_{k} is even, and that kk is an absolutely Galois MLF. Let π∈𝒪k\pi\in\mathcal{O}_{k} be a uniformizer of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. Let φ\varphi be the automorphism of GkG_{k} defined by the following equalities [cf. Theorem 1.2]:

φ⁡(σ)=σ,φ⁡(τ)=τ,φ⁡(x2)=x2​x1,φ⁡(xi)=xi​(i≠2).\displaystyle\varphi(\sigma)=\sigma,\ \varphi(\tau)=\tau,\ \varphi(x_{2})=x_{2}x_{1},\ \varphi(x_{i})=x_{i}\ (i\neq 2).

Then the continuous pkp_{k}-adic representation ρk,π∘φ\rho_{k,\pi}\circ\varphi is not Hodge-Tate.

On the other hand, in general, we cannot obtain an explicit automorphism of GkG_{k} that violates the Aut-intrinsic Hodge-Tate-ness of Lubin-Tate characters in the above proof of Corollary 3.6.

Remark 3.8.

Let pp be a prime number and ℚ¯p\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{p} an algebraic closure of ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}. Then it is well-known that the Lubin-Tate character over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} determined by the uniformizer pp coincides with the pp-adic cyclotomic character. Thus, the continuous pp-adic representations Gℚp=defGal⁡(ℚ¯p/ℚp)→ℚp×G_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{p}/\mathbb{Q}_{p})\to\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times} determined by the Lubin-Tate characters over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} [i.e., with respect to arbitrary choices of uniformizers of ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}] are Aut-intrinsically Hodge-Tate [cf. Remark 2.5; [11], Proposition 1.1]. This reflects a fundamental distinction between ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} and its nontrivial finite Galois extensions from the point of view of anabelian geometry [at least] in the case where p≥3p\geq 3.
